passages.t: The man who has seen affliction
passages.happening:
The third poem narrows to one person. ‘I am the man who has seen affliction under the rod of God’s wrath’ (verse 1). He does not name God for twenty verses. He only says He.

‘He has driven me away and made me walk in darkness instead of light’ (verse 2). God's hand is against him all day long. His flesh is worn away and his bones broken. ‘He has made me dwell in darkness like those dead for ages’ (verse 6). He is walled in and weighed down with chains. ‘Even when I cry out and plead for help, He shuts out my prayer’ (verse 8).

The pictures grow wilder. ‘He is a bear lying in wait, a lion hiding in ambush’ (verse 10). He is an archer, and the man is his target. ‘I am a laughingstock to all my people; they mock me in song all day long’ (verse 14). His mouth is full of gravel and his soul has forgotten what peace is.

So he says, ‘My strength has perished, along with my hope from the LORD’ (verse 18). That is the first time he names the LORD, and it is to say that his hope is gone. ‘Remember my affliction and wandering, the wormwood and the gall’ (verse 19). His soul remembers, and is bowed down within him (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
Chapters 1 and 2 spoke of the city. Now the ruin is felt in one body. The speaker may be a single sufferer such as Jeremiah, who was mocked all day long and later dropped into a muddy cistern during the siege. Or he may be an everyman, a figure who stands for the whole people. The chapter allows both, and readers have heard both.

Many of the pictures come from everyday life. The rod of verse 1 was the shepherd's or the parent's rod of discipline. Wormwood and gall were bitter plants, proverbial for anything bitter or poisonous. The pit, the darkness and the deep waters are also the language of the lament psalms, where they stand for the nearness of death.

This is the most elaborate acrostic in the Bible outside Psalm 119. It has sixty-six verses in twenty-two groups of three, and every verse in a group begins with the same Hebrew letter. The first hearers would have heard the alphabet marching on even while the man says he is walled in.

Notice what the man does not do. He does not pretend. He says God seems to be his enemy, and he says his hope from the LORD has perished. The Bible keeps these words.
passages.later: Jeremiah spoke almost the same words in his own anguish: ‘I am a laughingstock all day long; everyone mocks me’ (Jeremiah 20:7). Later he was lowered ‘into the cistern, which had no water but only mud’ (Jeremiah 38:6). And a psalm of lament prays from the same darkness: ‘You have laid me in the lowest Pit, in the darkest of the depths’ (Psalm 88:6).
passages.hard:
How can Scripture say that God shuts out prayer and tears a person to pieces?

The first twenty verses describe how affliction feels. God seems to be a bear, a lion, an archer, a jailer, one who will not listen. The Bible does not censor that experience. The psalms of lament, Psalms 13, 22 and 88 among them, speak the same way, and Job does too. The man is honest about his pain, and his honesty is not unbelief. He is still speaking to God, even while he says God will not hear.

The chapter does not leave him there. In the next verse he does something deliberate: he calls to mind what he knows of God's character, and that becomes the ground of his hope. But he says it in the dark, with nothing around him changed.

If this describes where you are right now, darkness without light and prayer that seems to hit a ceiling, you are not the first person of faith to be there.

If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line in your country. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The man names his pain fully before he names any hope. Ask whether you have let yourself do that, or whether you skip to the hope too quickly. And ask who in your life is in this darkness now, and whether they have anyone who will listen without hurrying them.

passages.t: Hope called to mind: mercies new every morning
passages.happening:
Then the turn. “Yet I call this to mind, and therefore I have hope: Because of the loving devotion of the LORD we are not consumed, for His mercies never fail. They are new every morning; great is Your faithfulness!” (verses 21-23).

For the first time he speaks to God directly, and it is praise. His soul says, ‘The LORD is my portion’ (verse 24), and so he will hope in him.

The poem now sounds like a wise teacher. ‘The LORD is good to those who wait for Him’ (verse 25). ‘It is good to wait quietly for the salvation of the LORD’ (verse 26). ‘It is good for a man to bear the yoke while he is still young’ (verse 27). Let him sit alone in silence, bury his face in the dust and ‘offer his cheek to the one who would strike him’ (verse 30).

‘For the Lord will not cast us off forever’ (verse 31). ‘Even if He causes grief, He will show compassion according to His abundant loving devotion’ (verse 32). ‘For He does not willingly afflict or grieve the sons of men’ (verse 33). To crush prisoners underfoot or deny a man justice in court, ‘of these the Lord does not approve’ (verse 36).

The passage ends with hard questions. Who speaks and it happens, unless the Lord has ordained it? ‘Do not both adversity and good come from the mouth of the Most High?’ (verse 38). Why should anyone complain, in view of his sins (verse 39)?
passages.hearers:
Nothing outside the man has changed between verse 18 and verse 21. The hope is not a feeling that arrives. It is a decision to call something to mind. He fixes his mind on what God has shown of himself.

Three Hebrew words carry the turn. Chesed, loving devotion, is loyal love within a covenant, love that keeps its promises when the other party has failed. Rachamim, mercies, is related to the word for womb and carries the sense of a mother's tender love for her child. Emunah, faithfulness, is the steadiness of someone who can be leaned on without giving way. There is a small question of text in verse 22: the standard Hebrew says the people are not consumed, and some ancient translations say that his mercies do not cease. Either way, God's loving devotion has not come to an end.

To call the LORD one's portion is the language of inheritance. When Israel entered the land, every tribe received a portion of land except the Levites, whose portion was the LORD himself. After the land has been lost, the man claims an inheritance no army can take.

These verses sit at the center of the whole book, and the book is built around them. The first hearers, surrounded by ruin, were given hope in the middle of the ruin, not after it.
passages.later: The same claim stands in a psalm: ‘God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever’ (Psalm 73:26). Waiting quietly is the posture of another psalm: ‘I wait for the LORD; my soul does wait, and in His word I put my hope’ (Psalm 130:5). And Isaiah promises the people, ‘My loving devotion will not depart from you’ (Isaiah 54:10).
passages.hard:
‘Do not both adversity and good come from the mouth of the Most High?’ (verse 38). If God does not willingly afflict, how can adversity come from him?

The chapter holds two things together and gives no neat theory. It says that nothing happens unless the Lord has ordained it (verses 37-38). It also says that he ‘does not willingly afflict or grieve the sons of men’ (verse 33), and that he does not approve of injustice (verse 36). Some readers stress the first: God is sovereign over all things, good and hard. Others stress the second: suffering is allowed within God's purposes but is not his heart's desire. Both readings agree that the man's honesty about his pain is not unbelief, and that his hope is chosen, not felt.

Verse 39 asks why anyone should complain in view of his sins. In its setting it is the city's confession about its own sin. It is not a word to say to someone else who is suffering, and it does not mean that any particular person's pain is a punishment. The whole book keeps complaining to God, and the Bible keeps those complaints.
passages.asks: The man says his hope has perished, and three verses later that he has hope. Ask what he did in between, and what that would look like for you. And ask what you know of God's character that you could call to mind on a dark morning.

passages.t: A call to examine and return, and tears until the LORD looks
passages.happening:
The voice changes to the people speaking together. ‘Let us examine and test our ways, and turn back to the LORD’ (verse 40). They lift their hearts and hands to God and confess, ‘We have sinned and rebelled; You have not forgiven’ (verse 42).

Then the confession turns into lament. God has covered himself in anger, pursued them and killed without pity (verse 43). ‘You have covered Yourself with a cloud that no prayer can pass through’ (verse 44). ‘You have made us scum and refuse among the nations’ (verse 45). Their enemies open their mouths against them, and panic and pitfall have come (verses 46-47).

The single voice returns, weeping. ‘Streams of tears flow from my eyes over the destruction of the daughter of my people’ (verse 48). His eyes overflow without relief, ‘until the LORD looks down from heaven and sees’ (verse 50).

He remembers his enemies. Without cause they hunted him like a bird. ‘They dropped me alive into a pit and cast stones upon me’ (verse 53). ‘The waters flowed over my head, and I thought I was going to die’ (verse 54).
passages.hearers:
The call to examine their ways is the communal heart of the chapter. After the hope of verses 21 to 39 comes repentance, and after repentance, honest lament again. The first hearers were given words to confess their sin as a people without being told that confession would make the pain go away at once.

Verse 42 is strikingly honest. The people confess, and in the same breath they say God has not yet forgiven. They do not hide the gap between their prayer and its answer.

Scum and refuse is the language of a people despised by its neighbors. After the fall, Judah lived under Babylonian rule at home and as deportees abroad, mocked by nations that had once feared it.

The pit with stones cast on it, and the waters over the head, could fit a prophet like Jeremiah, who was left in a muddy cistern during the siege. They are also the traditional pictures of the lament psalms, where the pit and the flood stand for the threat of death. The chapter allows the reader to hear both.
passages.later: A psalm of lament cries “Out of the depths I cry to You, O LORD!” (Psalm 130:1), and Jonah prays from the sea, ‘all Your breakers and waves swept over me’ (Jonah 2:3). The psalmist who sinks says, ‘I have drifted into deep waters, where the flood engulfs me’ (Psalm 69:2).
passages.asks: The people confess their sin and admit that forgiveness has not yet come. Ask whether you can pray honestly in that gap. And ask what it would mean to examine your own ways before you examine anyone else's.

passages.t: God heard from the pit, and a prayer for justice
passages.happening:
Now the man remembers that God answered. ‘I called on Your name, O LORD, out of the depths of the Pit’ (verse 55). God heard his plea. ‘You drew near when I called on You’ (verse 57), and God said, Do not be afraid. ‘You defend my cause, O Lord; You redeem my life’ (verse 58).

He asks God to finish what he has begun. ‘You have seen, O LORD, the wrong done to me’ (verse 59). God has seen all their malice and heard all their insults and plots (verses 60-62). They mock him in song when they sit and when they rise (verse 63).

The poem ends with a prayer for justice. ‘You will pay them back what they deserve, O LORD, according to the work of their hands’ (verse 64). He asks God to put anguish over their hearts, to curse them, and to pursue them in anger under heaven (verses 65-66).
passages.hearers:
The last part of the chapter moves from the pit to a remembered answer. Whether the man means a single rescue in the past, such as a prophet pulled out of a cistern, or the many times God had heard his people, the claim is the same. God drew near. The words Do not be afraid are the words God speaks again and again to his people in their fear.

The word redeem in verse 58, ga'al in Hebrew, belongs to Israel's family law. A redeemer was the near relative who stepped in to buy back land or to set free a family member. The man says God has acted for him as his nearest kin.

The prayer for justice at the end is spoken by a man who has been mocked, hunted and thrown into a pit. It does not take revenge into his own hands. It hands his enemies to God, who sees and judges by the work of their hands. The first hearers had real enemies who had done real harm, and the prayer gave them words for that too.
passages.later: God's word to his people, Do not be afraid, sounds through Isaiah: ‘do not be afraid, for I am your God. I will strengthen you; I will surely help you’ (Isaiah 41:10). A psalm prays from the same place: ‘You are my refuge, my portion in the land of the living’ (Psalm 142:5). And Paul tells believers not to avenge themselves but to ‘leave room for God’s wrath’ (Romans 12:19).
passages.asks: The man remembers that God drew near once, and that memory carries his prayer. Ask what times God has drawn near to you that you could remember in a dark season. And ask whether there is someone who wronged you whom you need to hand over to God rather than pursue yourself.
